title: How Skills and subagents work together in Legora
summary: Skills bring your team's expertise into the Legora Agent's work, while subagents handle separate tasks when independent execution improves the result.
body_markdown:
Legal work draws on several kinds of expertise at once. When reviewing an agreement, a lawyer applies legal knowledge alongside the team’s review method, the client’s negotiating positions, and drafting conventions. Those inputs inform one another, and all need to be considered in the wider context of the work being done.


[Skills](https://legora.com/blog/introducing-skills) help the Legora Agent work in a similar way. They allow legal teams to capture and deploy their standards and processes as reusable instructions and supporting materials for the Agent. Skills are modular: the Agent can call on a research methodology, report drafting guidelines, and a client communication style as needed, combining them to carry out an assignment.


Some parts of legal work benefit from separate execution. Legora uses subagents where that separation helps, including parallel investigations in[legal research](https://legora.com/product/legal-research) . Skills equip the Agent with reusable expertise; subagents allow it to delegate parts of an assignment. Adding expertise and dividing work are different design decisions.


## Applying team standards with Skills


A team might create a Skill for its agreement-review process, another for client-specific guidance, and a third for drafting conventions. Each can be maintained separately and reused across assignments.


The Agent applies those Skills together during a review. The review instructions guide what to examine, the client’s negotiating positions inform the recommendation, and the drafting conventions shape how it is expressed.


This modularity allows the same drafting Skill to support an agreement review, a research report, or a client update. Teams can refine each body of guidance independently and combine it with others as the assignment requires. Applying another area of expertise does not, by itself, require a separate worker.


## Using subagents where they improve the outcome


Some assignments benefit from dividing work. A legal research question spanning several jurisdictions, for example, can be broken into separate investigations that proceed in parallel.


Legora uses subagents for this kind of research. Each receives a task and relevant context, then returns focused findings for the Agent to bring into the wider analysis. A separate working context can also keep extensive intermediate research from overwhelming the main analysis.


## Choosing when to delegate


Asking a colleague to investigate a separate jurisdiction can be a sensible division of work. Asking another colleague to take over a review solely to apply a writing style introduces a handoff for something the reviewing lawyer could apply directly. In either case, delegation requires a brief and a way to incorporate the returned work.


The same considerations apply to agents. Each subagent needs enough context to carry out its task, and its findings must be incorporated into the wider analysis. These steps can require additional model calls and tokens. If relevant information is omitted from the brief or the findings returned, the quality of the completed work can also suffer.


Legora evaluates whether the benefits of separate execution justify the coordination it requires. We assess the complete assignment: the quality of the answer, how long it takes, the resources it uses, and how much review and correction it requires.


Skills and subagents give us complementary ways to improve that result. Expertise can be specialized and reused without requiring a separate worker for every specialty. Where independent execution adds value, the Agent can delegate. Our approach is to apply expertise within the ongoing work and introduce a separate worker when doing so improves the outcome.
